Epictetus - Wikipedia
Contents
Epictetus
Epictetus
(
/
ˌ
ɛ
p
ɪ
k
ˈ
t
iː
t
ə
s
/
EH
-pick-
TEE
-təss
;
[
4
]
Ancient Greek
:
Ἐπίκτητος
,
Epíktētos
;
c.
50
–
c.
135 AD) was a Greek
Stoic philosopher
.
[
5
]
[
6
]
He was born
into slavery
at
Hierapolis
,
Phrygia
(present-day
Pamukkale
, in western
Turkey
) and lived in
Rome
until his banishment, after which he spent the rest of his life in
Nicopolis
in northwestern
Greece
.
Epictetus studied Stoic philosophy under
Musonius Rufus
and after
manumission
, his formal emancipation from slavery, he began to teach philosophy. When philosophers were banished from Rome by Emperor
Domitian
toward the end of the first century, Epictetus founded a school of philosophy in
Nicopolis
. He taught that philosophy is
a way of life
and not simply a theoretical discipline. To Epictetus, all external events are
beyond our control
; he argues that we should accept whatever happens calmly and dispassionately. However, he held that individuals are
responsible for their own actions
, which they can examine and control through rigorous self-discipline. His teachings were written down and published by his pupil
Arrian
in his
Discourses
and
Enchiridion
. They influenced many later thinkers, including
Marcus Aurelius
,
Rabelais
,
Pascal
,
Montesquieu
,
Diderot
, and
Samuel Johnson
.
Life
Having described himself as old in AD
108, Epictetus is presumed to have been born around AD 50,
[
7
]
[
8
]
at
Hierapolis
,
Phrygia
.
[
9
]
The name given by his parents is unknown. The name by which he is known is derived from the word
epíktētos
(ἐπίκτητος) that in
Greek
, simply means "gained" or "acquired";
[
10
]
the Greek philosopher
Plato
, in his
Laws
, used that term to mean property that is "added to one's hereditary property".
[
11
]
Epictetus spent his youth in Rome as a
slave
to
Epaphroditus
, a wealthy
freedman
who was secretary to
Nero
.
[
12
]
Epictetus's social position was thus complicated, combining the low status of a slave with the high status of one with a personal connection to imperial power.
[
13
]
Early in life, Epictetus acquired a passion for philosophy and, with the permission of his wealthy master, he studied
Stoic
philosophy under
Musonius Rufus
.
[
14
]
Becoming more educated in this way raised his social status.
[
15
]
At some point, he became disabled.
Celsus
, quoted by
Origen
, wrote that this was because his leg had been deliberately broken by his master.
[
16
]
Without citing a cause,
Simplicius
wrote that Epictetus had been disabled from childhood.
[
17
]
Epictetus obtained his freedom sometime after the death of Nero in AD 68,
[
18
]
and he began to teach
philosophy
in Rome. Around AD 93, when the
Roman emperor
Domitian
banished all philosophers from the city,
[
19
]
Epictetus moved to
Nicopolis
in
Epirus
,
Greece
, where he founded a school of philosophy.
[
20
]
His most famous pupil,
Arrian
, studied under him as a young man (around AD 108) and claimed to have written his famous
Discourses
based on the notes he took about lectures by Epictetus. Arrian argued that his Discourses should be considered comparable to the
Socratic
literature.
[
21
]
Arrian described Epictetus as a powerful speaker who could "induce his listener to feel just what Epictetus wanted him to feel".
[
22
]
Many eminent figures sought conversations with him.
[
23
]
Emperor
Hadrian
was friendly with him,
[
24
]
possibly having heard Epictetus speak at his school in Nicopolis.
[
25
]
[
26
]
Epictetus lived a life of great
simplicity
, with few possessions.
[
17
]
He lived alone for a long time,
[
27
]
but in his old age, he adopted the child of a friend who otherwise would have been left to die, and raised him with the aid of a woman.
[
28
]
It is unclear whether Epictetus and she were married.
[
29
]
He died sometime around AD 135.
[
30
]
After his death, according to
Lucian
, his
oil lamp
was purchased by an admirer for 3,000
drachmae
.
[
31
]
Thought
Epictetus maintains that the foundation of all philosophy is
self-knowledge
; that is, the conviction of our ignorance and gullibility ought to be the first subject of our study.
[
32
]
Logic
provides valid reasoning and certainty in judgment, but it is subordinate to practical needs.
[
33
]
He also maintained that the first and most necessary part of philosophy concerns the application of doctrine, for example, that people should not
lie
. The second concerns reasons, e.g., why people should not lie. The third, lastly, examines and establishes the reasons.
[
34
]
This is the logical part, which finds reasons, shows what is a reason, and that a given reason is a correct one.
[
34
]
This last part is necessary, but only on account of the second, which again is rendered necessary by the first.
[
35
]
Legacy
No writings by Epictetus are known. His discourses were transcribed and compiled by his pupil
Arrian
(
c.
86/89
– c.
after 146/160 AD
).
[
22
]
The main work is
The Discourses
, four books of which have been preserved (out of the original eight).
[
36
]
Arrian also compiled a popular digest, entitled the
Enchiridion
, or
Handbook
, of Epictetus. In a preface to the
Discourses
that is addressed to Lucius Gellius, Arrian states that "whatever I heard him say I used to write down, word for word, as best I could, endeavouring to preserve it as a memorial, for my own future use, of his way of thinking and the frankness of his speech".
[
22
]
Some scholars, however, have doubted this claim and suggest that Epictetus in fact wrote the
Discourses
himself, though it is not the consensus opinion.
[
37
]
The philosophy of Epictetus influenced the Roman emperor
Marcus Aurelius
(AD 121 to 180), who cites Epictetus in his
Meditations
.
[
38
]
Epictetus also appears in a second or third century
Dialogue Between the Emperor Hadrian and Epictetus the Philosopher
.
[
39
]
This short Latin text consists of seventy-three short questions supposedly posed by
Hadrian
and answered by Epictetus.
[
39
]
This dialogue was very popular in the
Middle Ages
with many translations and adaptations.
[
39
]
Epictetus exhibited an influence on French
Enlightenment
philosophers, such as
Voltaire
,
Montesquieu
,
Denis Diderot
, and
Baron d'Holbach
, who all read the
Enchiridion
when they were students.
[
40
]
Blaise Pascal
listed Epictetus as among those philosophers he was most familiar with, describing him as a "great mind" who is "among the philosophers of the world who have best understood the duties" of an individual.
[
41
]
In the sixth century, the
Neoplatonist
philosopher
Simplicius
wrote an extant commentary on the
Enchiridion
.
[
42
]
